articles.title: DMK Women’s Wing to stage Statewide protest over law and order on October 31, says Stalin
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: The DMK Women’s Wing will stage a a Statewide demonstration on October 31 to condemn the deteriorating law and order in Tamil Nadu, the party president, M.K. Stalin, has said.

Mr. Stalin pointed to the recent criminal incidents in Tamil Nadu. “In Salem, a murder took place in broad daylight in public space. In Madurai, a missing boy was found dead. The whereabouts of the missing girl from Gingee remain a mystery. Crimes in Tamil Nadu are escalating to a degree that surpasses video games and horror films. Under TVK rule, criminals are carrying out offences without fear, as though they had been given a free run. Tamil Nadu is in the grim state of counting murders every single day. Why is the Chief Minister remaining silent, as if he had nothing to do with law and order? Why is he, who is adept at talking loudly about law and order, not opening his mouth,” he asked.
To condemn this situation, the DMK Women’s Wing would stage the demonstration, he said.

articles.title: Former DMK Minister Anbil Mahesh Poyyamozhi arrested in ₹100 crore private schools fraud case
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Hours after his anticipatory bail plea was dismissed by the Madras High Court on Monday (October 26, 2026), former DMK Minister Anbil Mahesh Poyyamozhi was arrested by the Chennai police in connection with an alleged multicrore scam.

According to police sources, a special team of the Central Crime Brach (CCB) investigating allegations that several crores of rupees were collected as ‘party fund’ from various private school managements across Tamil Nadu arrested Mr. Poyyamozhi who was the School Education Minister between 2021 and 2026.
Investigation reveals collection of ‘party fund’ during Anbil Mahesh Poyyamozhi’s tenure as School Education Minister, CCB tells Madras High Court
Anbil Mahesh Poyyamozhi gave reassurance to family members of absconding accused, CCB tells Madras High Court

The case arises out of a complaint lodged by C. Elangovan, secretary of Tamil Nadu Private Schools Federation, with the Chennai Police Commissioner levelling serious charges against B.T. Arasakumar (59) who was accused of having collected large sums of money by running an unregistered association named ‘Tamil Nadu Private Schools Association’

The complainant alleged that Mr. Arasakumar, who was later detained under the Goondas Act, had collected money from private school managements by promising to offer services such as obtaining approvals for upgrading schools, gaining permanent recognition, securing building plan approvals etc “using his proximity” with the then ruling dispensation, the sources said.

The CCB had included Mr. Poyyamozhi as an accused in the case only after seizing evidence which pointed to collection of bribe money termed as ‘party fund’. Muthukumar, alleged to be a close associate of Mr. Poyyamozhi, was absconding and efforts were on to apprehend him at the earliest, the sources said.

articles.title: J&K Cabinet expansion, swearing-in on October 27
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: The expansion of the Jammu and Kashmir Council of Ministers headed by Chief Minister Omar Abdullah will take place in Srinagar on Tuesday (October 27, 2026), party officials said.

"The oath-taking ceremony for the new ministers is scheduled to take place at 10.30 am on Tuesday (October 27, 2026)," National Conference spokesperson Tanvir Sadiq told reporters in Srinagar on Monday (October 26, 2026).
Mr. Sadiq said the party leadership, including Omar Abdullah and party president Farooq Abdullah, will decide on the new faces to be inducted into the Council of Ministers.
"I think by this evening it will be clear as to who all are being sworn in tomorrow," he added.

The Chief Minister on Saturday (October 24, 2026) called on Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha and sought time for swearing in new Ministers as part of reshuffle and expansion in the Council of Ministers.
Asked about the controversial statement regarding Pakistan made by Mr. Farooq Abdullah, the NC spokesperson said that the statement was taken "out of context".

"If you listen to the entire speech, he (Farooq Abdullah) made it clear how the tribal invaders came here and the injustices that emanated from the neighbouring country against Jammu and Kashmir. This is just petty politics being played by the BJP when they take out one part of the speech and present it out of context," he added.

articles.title: Pakistan’s Punjab government extends detention of Imran Khan’s sisters by 30 days
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: The Punjab government in Pakistan has extended the detention of jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan's three sisters for another 30 days under a public safety law, an official said on Monday (October 26, 2026).
Aleema Khan, Noreen Niazi and Dr. Uzma Khan have been detained at Lahore's Kot Lakhpat Jail for over a month under the Punjab Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance, 1960.

While Ms. Aleema was detained on September 20, 2026, Ms. Uzma and Ms. Noreen were taken into custody the following day, amid a crackdown on efforts to mobilise support for the jailed Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) founder.

An assistant advocate general of Punjab informed the Lahore High Court (LHC) on Monday that the government had extended the detention of Mr. Khan's three sisters for another 30 days, on the recommendation of the Lahore deputy commissioner.
The court subsequently disposed of a petition seeking the trio's release. The petition was filed by Ms. Aleema's son, Shahrez, challenging the detention of the sisters.
Rana Mudassar Umar, counsel for the petitioner, told the court last week that the three sisters remained in jail despite the expiry of the 30-day detention period on October 20, 2026.
Subsequently, Lahore High Court Justice Abher Gul Khan directed the Punjab home secretary and the Kot Lakhpat jail superintendent to appear at the next hearing and submit their replies.

The sisters were detained amid PTI's efforts to organise nationwide protests demanding Mr. Khan's release. The former Prime Minister, 74, has been in jail since August 2023 and faces multiple cases, which he and his party have described as politically motivated.

PTI leaders criticised the Punjab government, led by Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz, over the extension of the detention orders, questioning the need to hold the sisters when, they said, they were not wanted in any criminal case.
Former federal minister and PTI leader Moonis Elahi termed the detention illegal, alleging that the government was using preventive detention to target the party and its leadership.

"Preventive detention cannot be used as a substitute for ordinary criminal law. Their detention is politically motivated and part of a wider crackdown on the party and its leadership," he said, calling for the sisters' immediate release.

articles.title: Coimbatore school student’s death case: probe transferred to CB-CID
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: Director General of Police Mahesh Kumar Aggarwal transferred the investigation into the alleged death by suicide of Class XI student A. Akilan (16) in Coimbatore to the Crime Bran Criminal Investigation Department (CB-CID) on Monday (October 26, 2026).

The DGP’s order stated that the case, which was registered by the Peelamedu police in Coimbatore under Sections 115(2), 108 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita read with 3(2)(v) of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act in connection with the death on October 22, has been transferred to the CB-CID for further investigation.

The order directed the Coimbatore City Police Commissioner to hand over the original case file and all connected records of the case to the DGP, CB-CID, immediately. The DGP, CB-CID, will nominate an investigating officer, who will take up the investigation.

Personnel from the city police handed over a copy of the order to family members of the deceased, who along with relatives and members of various political parties and organisations have been staging a protest near South Taluk office for the past few days, demanding arrest of all persons who abetted the suicide.

Akilan, who belongs to a Scheduled Caste community, was found dead in his house on October 21. The police arrested two of his classmates , who belong to different dominant castes, two days later for allegedly having subjected him to caste-based harassment. The police were also investigating allegations levelled by Akilan’s mother against a teacher and the headmaster.
(Assistance for overcoming suicidal thoughts is available on the State’s health helpline 104, Tele-MANAS 14416, and Sneha’s suicide prevention helpline 044-24640050.)

articles.title: ‘No understanding of nationalism’: West Bengal CM Suvendu Adhikari slams TMC
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II: Polity, Governance, Supreme Court Judgements, Bills & Govt Schemes
fullParagraphs: West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari on Monday (October 26, 2026) slammed the previous Trinamool Congress government for allegedly indulging in appeasement politics, claiming that it had "no understanding of nationalism" and planned to turn the State into "greater Bangladesh".
Mr. Adhikari also accused the previous government of composing a separate song for the State, designing a flag and adopting the 'Joy Bangla' slogan of the neighbouring country.

Speaking to reporters in Tamluk, West Bengal, after a ' bhoomi pujan ' for a BJP party office, the Chief Minister said, "The previous government in Bengal had no understanding of nationalism, engaged in appeasement politics, and planned to turn the state into greater Bangladesh."
"That is why they had composed a separate song for the state, designed a flag and adopted the 'Joy Bangla' slogan of Bangladesh," he said.
Mr. Adhikari urged the people to remain united and stand with Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

Taking a dig at the Cockroach Janta Party for its protests over alleged irregularities in the SIR exercise, the CM appealed to the people to make sure that the ' Dimagi Naxal ', ' tukde tukde ' gangs, cockroaches and termites "do not breed" in Bengal.

articles.title: UPI and the cost of policy reversal
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The government has just given itself the legal room to tax the very payment habit it spent a decade building. Tucked into the Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2026, is an amendment to Section 10A of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, which would allow the government to notify charges on specified electronic payment modes. The number being proposed is a Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) of 0.25–0.5% on UPI transactions above ₹2,000. The official stand is that this threshold would touch only about five per cent of transactions by volume, sparing the milk-and-vegetable payments that make up the bulk of UPI’s use. But it would cover roughly 65% of transaction value, which is precisely why it matters.
This is not a small, technical fix. It runs counter to a decade-long policy commitment and deserves more scrutiny than it has received.

Consider the arc. Demonetisation in November 2016 was justified, among other things, as a push towards a less-cash economy. UPI, launched earlier that year, became the vehicle for that push, and its zero-MDR regime was a deliberate subsidy to get merchants and consumers off cash. It worked spectacularly. UPI now processes more transactions each month than most of the world’s card networks combined. Having successfully weaned the country away from cash and towards electronic payments, the government now wants to undercut the very success it engineered.

There seems to be a continued pattern of privileging one payment mode over others via policy. India has long taxed even credit cards. Credit card interest and fees attract 18% GST, making the use of credit cards unnecessarily costly. Taxing interest on revolving credit is unusual by international standards; most jurisdictions treat consumer credit interest as a private financial cost, not a taxable service. India taxes it as if using a credit card itself is a luxury.

Now UPI, the payment rail the government spent political capital promoting, is in line for similar treatment. The pattern suggests a need for a more coherent payments policy than giving in to the temptation to tax every transaction that can be observed.
There are at least two problems with this specific move beyond the optics.

First, basic economic theory tells us that the person on whom a tax is levied and the person who actually bears its cost are not always the same. Moreover, UPI or any payments interface is a two-sided market, and taxing two-sided markets is genuinely tricky.

The MDR would nominally fall on merchants, as argued by the government, collected via banks and the National Payments Corporation of India’s ecosystem. But whether that cost gets passed through to merchants, on to consumers, or absorbed by banks and payment service providers depends on competitive intensity on each side of the market. Banks and fintechs compete for merchant relationships and cannot easily raise prices without losing volume to a rival offering free UPI acceptance.

The more likely outcome is that intermediaries — the banks and PSPs that built and maintain the plumbing — absorb the cost, which erodes their incentive to invest in reliability, fraud prevention and expansion into underserved segments. A tax that cannot be reliably passed through does not disappear; it most likely shows up later as degraded service or slower innovation. This is completely counterintuitive if government is proposing this tax as necessary to fund the next stage of UPI growth.

Second, UPI has done real work on financial inclusion at the margin. It has pulled informal transactions into a recorded, traceable digital trail — the very outcome that formalisation and tax-compliance advocates have wanted for years. There have also been attempts to provide credit based on the digital trail created by electronic payments. Every rupee that moves through UPI instead of cash is a rupee the financial institutions can eventually see and use to build a spending profile.

Charging the rail directly could undercut the incentive to use it, cutting against long-standing financial inclusion goals. The government does not need to raise revenue from every rupee that moves electronically; it needs those rupees to keep moving electronically, because that is what delivers the inclusion and compliance dividends it has been chasing since 2016.

Ideally, which payment mode to adopt should be an economic decision for participating actors. Factors such as the size of the business, consumer preferences, and relative cost of using alternative payment systems should determine their usage. Deliberate policy intervention and the current government’s war on cash tilted the scales in favour of UPI. Taxing it now — however nominal or small — could change its usage patterns, and policymakers should not be surprised if one outcome is reduced UPI usage.

articles.title: How India’s life insurance sector funds government expenditure
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: When the government borrows, the question that follows is rarely asked aloud: who lends? A large part of the answer is the life insurance sector. Every year, millions of households across India pay premiums into life insurance policies. That money is reinvested, for decades, in the very securities that finance government expenditure — roads, railways, water supplies, hospitals, defence. The household protecting itself against the loss of its breadwinner is simultaneously, and unknowingly, lending to the sovereign [the Central government]. Life insurers collectively hold close to a quarter of India’s outstanding central government dated securities, based on RBI and IRDAI data — a share that has remained stable even as the total sovereign debt stock expanded by around 40 per cent in three years. This is not a number that appears in budget speeches or parliamentary debates. It is, however, a number that matters.

The stoic and resilient quality of the sector’s sovereign support is as significant as its scale. Life insurers write policies with tenures of twenty, thirty, sometimes forty years. Government securities are the natural habitat of long-duration liabilities — the only asset class that absorbs this scale of funds at matching tenures without distorting the market. Unlike foreign portfolio investors, whose appetite fluctuates with global risk sentiment, insurance companies buy and hold. They do not exit when oil prices rise or when a geopolitical event triggers a reassessment of emerging market exposure. Their participation is counter-cyclical by design — stable precisely when other buyers become unreliable. A steady domestic base of long-horizon holders reduces rollover risk and moderates borrowing costs across the maturity spectrum.
Life insurers buy when others sell, hold when others exit, and reinvest when others pause. That is the structural consequence of writing long-duration promises to millions of policyholders.

The sector’s contribution is not evenly distributed. The Life Insurance Corporation of India carries the dominant share — a consequence of its scale, its predominantly participating product mix, and the duration of its in-force book. Its March 2025 regulatory filing with IRDAI (Form L-26) confirms that sovereign paper accounts for nearly 63 per cent of its non-linked policyholder corpus — well above the regulatory minimum, and a direct expression of what long-duration liabilities demand at scale.

LIC holds approximately 19 per cent of all outstanding central government dated securities — a figure confirmed by the RBI’s Public Debt Management Quarterly Report for FY24, the most recently published data. LIC’s IRDAI regulatory filings for March 2025 give the institutional reality in absolute terms: ₹20.2 lakh crore in central government securities alone, and ₹32.3 lakh crore in total government and government-guaranteed securities across all funds. These are not estimates. They are figures LIC files with its regulator every quarter and that any researcher can access on the IRDAI website. This makes LIC the single largest institutional holder of Indian government’s debt.
Government securities are the natural habitat of long-duration liabilities — the only asset class that absorbs this scale of funds at matching tenures without distorting the market.

Private life insurers, with a higher proportion of unit-linked and shorter-tenure products, contribute a smaller fraction today. As they grow and deepen their traditional offerings, their sovereign allocations will follow the same structural logic.

The regulator has already recognised the systemic dimension of this function: IRDAI designates LIC as a Domestic Systemically Important Insurer every year, describing it as an institution whose distress would cause significant dislocation in the financial system. That designation, rightly made on insurance-sector grounds, points toward a wider truth — the dislocation would extend into the sovereign borrowing programme itself.

Insurers in Japan, the United Kingdom, and South Korea are among the largest holders of their respective governments’ long-dated securities, not because regulation mandates it but because their liability profiles demand it. India’s life insurance sector is following the same path.

India’s life insurance penetration stood at 2.7 per cent of GDP in FY25, the third consecutive year of decline from a pandemic-era peak of 3.2 per cent, against a global life average of 3.0 per cent. Three regulatory interventions between 2023 and 2024 — restructured distribution economics, taxation on certain high-value policies, and mandatory product repricing, simultaneously, has compressed new businesses. While each was defensible in isolation, their cumulative effect was adverse. The sector is recovering. But the episode illustrates a risk worth noting: when multiple regulatory actions compress new business at once, the household savings that would otherwise have flowed into the sovereign debt market through insurance, reduce or find shorter-duration homes elsewhere. The sovereign borrowing programme may not notice this in the short term. Over a decade, it would.
Banking commands policy attention in proportion to its systemic importance. Insurance, which quietly holds close to a quarter of outstanding central government dated securities, does not.

The case for deeper insurance penetration is most often made in the language of household financial protection — the uninsured family, the inadequate sum assured, a mis-sold product or an unsettled claim. These are legitimate concerns. But there is a parallel case, made in the language of sovereign fiscal stability, that has not been fully articulated in public policy discourse. If the reliability of India’s domestic sovereign funding base is a macroeconomic priority given the scale of annual borrowing requirements, then the depth and health of the life insurance sector remain directly relevant to that priority.

articles.title: Swiping in dark: The hidden cost of plastic money
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: A smartwatch bought on impulse, a costly phone ordered just for the thrill of owning it, a festive sale too tempting to resist. In isolation, each swipe may seem harmless, yet the danger lies in accumulation. Money spent in moments of desire can quietly turn into a burden that outlasts the fleeting gratification. Small indulgences, if they add up to a sizeable bill, can take a toll on the monthly budget and derail carefully planned financial goals.
The litmus test comes knocking much later, after the swipes have ended: a shocking bill. Now, to overcome the shock, cardholders often look for a shortcut: paying just the minimum due.

The minimum-due loop is one of the most deceptive traps of a credit card. Paying only this negligible fraction may help avert immediate late-payment penalties and default notices. However, it allows the bulk of your debt to linger and compound.

Crucially, carrying a due attracts interest and simultaneously revokes the interest-free grace period for subsequent purchases. Any new spend begins accruing interest charges immediately at typical annual rates of 36% to 42%, compounded monthly, until the entire bill is cleared in full. If the minimum-due route is a slow leak, ignoring the bill payment entirely is an outright rupture. Failing to pay the minimum due carries far more severe consequences.

The bank would immediately flag the account as overdue, levying hefty late-payment penalties on top of the standard charges. If the default crosses a stipulated time, the bank reports the delinquency to CIBIL and other credit bureaus, leaving a long-lasting scar on your score.

When the bill is bulky, cardholders often lean towards another tempting escape hatch: easy EMIs. Converting a purchase into equated monthly instalments does not erase the cost; rather, it locks you into a high-margin contract.
You forfeit the upfront discounts that are often bundled with full payment, while a relentless 18% GST is slapped onto the interest portion of every single EMI.
By splitting past impulse purchases across future months, you silently mortgage your upcoming cash flows. The bitter truth: the thrill of owning fades fast, but the bill of burden goes on and on.

Paying your bill on time is only half the battle. Even if you are punctual in clearing the bills, it’s not a total financial hygiene. When the usage on your card is close to its ceiling, you trigger an alarm button inside credit bureaus. Lenders gauge your financial stability through credit utilisation, and crossing the 30% threshold paints a picture of being cash hungry. Even if you do not default payment, a high usage of credit erodes your CIBIL score rating, transforming routine swipes into a hidden roadblock when you eventually apply for a home or vehicle loan.
Gliding your credit card smoothly into an ATM for quick cash would force you to endure a rough patch with huge money leaks.

On most credit cards, cash withdrawals carry zero grace period, meaning standard interest rates of 36 to 42% begin compounding moments after the currency is dispensed. Even on select promotional cards that tout an interest-free window, the fixed fees bite hard.

For instance, banks usually cap single ATM withdrawals at ₹10,000 while levying a flat processing fee of around ₹199 plus GST on every single attempt. Therefore, a requirement of ₹50,000 forces you to glide into the vending tunnel five times, instantly draining roughly over ₹1,000 in raw processing charges alone.

articles.title: Ethanol tender sparks feedstock concerns as rice gains ground over maize
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: The Oil Marketing Companies’ (OMCs) latest ethanol procurement tender for Ethanol Supply Year (ESY) 2026–27 has triggered concerns among grain-based ethanol producers and sections of the sugar industry over feedstock pricing, allocation priorities and the potential implications for the sector.

The tender sets procurement prices at ₹60.32 a litre for surplus foodgrains (SFG), with a stated cap of 108 crore litres for the first three quarters; ₹64 a litre for damaged foodgrains (DFG); and ₹66 a litre for maize, plus an additional ₹2.79 a litre. While ethanol produced from sugarcane juice, sugar syrup and B-heavy molasses has been excluded, C-heavy molasses-based ethanol remains eligible for procurement.

The Grain Ethanol Manufacturers Association (GEMA) has argued that the tender places a disproportionate burden on rice-based feedstocks, particularly SFG and DFG, while potentially weakening maize’s role as an industrial feedstock.
The pricing differential has also created uncertainty over how procurement demand will be distributed among the different feedstock categories.

According to industry estimates, DFG-based ethanol allocation during ESY 2025–26 was approximately 60 crore litres. For ESY 2026–27, the industry anticipates that the allocation could exceed 700 crore litres.

C.K. Jain, president of GEMA, said a balanced ethanol policy must support viable production from both maize and rice, with procurement prices reflecting their different cost structures and allocations providing reasonable visibility to producers. He added that the government and OMCs should review the pricing and allocation framework.

GEMA has also questioned whether maize will receive adequate procurement opportunities under the lowest-price-based allocation mechanism. It has called for greater clarity on the methodology for feedstock-wise allocation and the role envisaged for maize in meeting the country’s ethanol requirements.

The Indian Sugar & Bio-Energy Manufacturers Association (ISMA) has welcomed the exclusion of ethanol produced from sugarcane juice, sugar syrup and B-heavy molasses, arguing that the approach is consistent with the need to safeguard domestic sugar availability amid uncertainty over the forthcoming crop.
C-heavy molasses-based ethanol, it noted, allows sugar mills to continue contributing to the ethanol-blending programme without diverting recoverable sugar.
However, ISMA has raised concerns over the preferential allocation granted to dedicated ethanol plants holding Long-Term Offtake Agreements under the ESY 2026–27 tender.
While the provision is already in place for the current year, its continuation in subsequent years could hurt the sugar industry, the association said.

articles.title: Data suggests broad-based increase in food prices: RBI Bulletin
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Banking/SSC: RBI Monetary Policy, GDP, Inflation, Budget & Banking
fullParagraphs: High-frequency data collected by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) for October (till 19th), suggest a broad-based increase in food prices, said RBI officials in the October edition of RBI Bulletin, which was released on Friday (October 23, 2026).

“Among cereals, rice and wheat prices continued to increase. Prices of major pulses also went up sequentially. Edible oil prices also recorded a slow and broad-based increase, led by mustard and palm oil,” they wrote in the ‘State of the Economy’ article.
Among vegetables, while potato prices declined and the pace of onion price increases dropped, tomato prices picked up, they added.

Surprisingly, inflation in rural areas has been getting higher than that in urban areas. Inflation stood at 4.9% and 6.1%, respectively, in urban and rural areas in September. In August, urban and rural inflation stood at 4.3% and 5.2% respectively, the officials stated.
ALSO WATCH The battle against inflation is entering a tougher phase: What it means for you

The majority of States/UTs recorded inflation in the range of 4-6% in September. Inflation ranged from 2.9% to 6.9% across states/UTs. States like Telangana, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry recorded inflation in excess of 6% across both rural and urban areas, they pointed out.

Stating that WPI inflation recorded its first double-digit rate in the new series (Base 2022-23) at 11.4% in September 2026, rising from 9.9% in August, reflecting a broad-based increase in prices, they said industrial and farm input costs remained elevated.
Inflation in the Output Producer Price Index surged to 11.4% in September 2026 from 9.8% in August, led by manufacturing products, and mining & quarrying, they said.
As per the article headline, CPI inflation edged up over the months and showed signs of greater generalisation across commodities, calling for a commensurate change in the monetary policy stance.
“The external headwinds are also being dealt with a slew of regulatory measures by the Reserve Bank to curb speculative activity in foreign exchange market,” they stated.

“Strong inflows under FCNR(B) swap window augmented reserves. Foreign Direct Investment (FDI), External Commercial Borrowing (ECB) and remittance flows strengthened in August. With strong exports growth, the trade deficit narrowed in September,” they added.

The headline Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation rose to a 23-month high of 5.5% (YoY) in September from 4.8% in August, driven by a broad-based increase in food, fuel and core (CPI excluding food and fuel) components.

Its peer Hindustan Petroleum had reported a 9% decline in standalone net profits on Thursday.
Delhi-headquartered peer Indian Oil is scheduled to post their September-end financial results on October 30.

articles.title: Pakistan’s Punjab government extends detention of Imran Khan’s sisters by 30 days
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: The Punjab government in Pakistan has extended the detention of jailed former Prime Minister Imran Khan's three sisters for another 30 days under a public safety law, an official said on Monday (October 26, 2026).
Aleema Khan, Noreen Niazi and Dr. Uzma Khan have been detained at Lahore's Kot Lakhpat Jail for over a month under the Punjab Maintenance of Public Order Ordinance, 1960.

While Ms. Aleema was detained on September 20, 2026, Ms. Uzma and Ms. Noreen were taken into custody the following day, amid a crackdown on efforts to mobilise support for the jailed Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) founder.

An assistant advocate general of Punjab informed the Lahore High Court (LHC) on Monday that the government had extended the detention of Mr. Khan's three sisters for another 30 days, on the recommendation of the Lahore deputy commissioner.
The court subsequently disposed of a petition seeking the trio's release. The petition was filed by Ms. Aleema's son, Shahrez, challenging the detention of the sisters.
Rana Mudassar Umar, counsel for the petitioner, told the court last week that the three sisters remained in jail despite the expiry of the 30-day detention period on October 20, 2026.
Subsequently, Lahore High Court Justice Abher Gul Khan directed the Punjab home secretary and the Kot Lakhpat jail superintendent to appear at the next hearing and submit their replies.

The sisters were detained amid PTI's efforts to organise nationwide protests demanding Mr. Khan's release. The former Prime Minister, 74, has been in jail since August 2023 and faces multiple cases, which he and his party have described as politically motivated.

PTI leaders criticised the Punjab government, led by Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz, over the extension of the detention orders, questioning the need to hold the sisters when, they said, they were not wanted in any criminal case.
Former federal minister and PTI leader Moonis Elahi termed the detention illegal, alleging that the government was using preventive detention to target the party and its leadership.

"Preventive detention cannot be used as a substitute for ordinary criminal law. Their detention is politically motivated and part of a wider crackdown on the party and its leadership," he said, calling for the sisters' immediate release.

articles.title: Iran says resumption of war would not change its stances
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday (October 25, 2026) that a potential resumption of war with Israel and the United States would not change his country's positions.

The remarks come amid mounting U.S and Israeli threats of renewed attacks on Iran , as President Donald Trump said on Friday (October 23, 2026) that Washington "may do another little Epic Fury," referring to the U.S-Israeli campaign on Iran that began on February 28 .

"Recently, there has been talk of a new war, but I am already thinking about the post-war period. Whether there is war or not, our policies remain the same," said Mr. Araghchi during a televised event in Tehran.
"They have already done so twice and have seen the results. If they want to try again, they know they will achieve no different outcome from those of the past," he added.

An April 8 ceasefire between Iran and the United States put an end to the most intense fighting, apart from sporadic exchanges of fire in and around the strategic Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy supplies.

Iran has claimed control over Strait of Hormuz since the outbreak of the war and has regularly targeted vessels that attempt crossing without its authorisation, moves strongly opposed by Washington and countries in the region.
In response, the U.S has been maintaining a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports.

In June, Iran agreed with the United States to a memorandum of understanding laying out a pathway to a permanent settlement of the conflict, only for the deal to later unravel as each side accused the other of violating it.
Tehran has since called for a return to the accord to end the conflict.

articles.title: Lula wins a record fourth presidential term as Brazil defeats far-right, defies Trump and Meta
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: In an election campaign that may be recorded in history for countering far-right tactics, defying foreign interference and social media manipulation, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva secured a historic fourth presidential term, defeating Flávio Bolsonaro of Liberal Party (PL) in Brazil’s runoff elections on Sunday (October 25, 2026). Mr. Lula secured 64 million votes, the highest total ever recorded in a Brazilian presidential election, surpassing his own record of 60 million votes he received in 2022.

Declaring a “defeat for lies and denialism”, he pledged to govern for all Brazilians and protect the country’s sovereignty. “Brazil is nobody’s backyard,” Mr. Lula declared at a midnight rally, sending a clear message to U.S. president Donald Trump as he addressed hundreds of thousands of supporters gathered along São Paulo’s iconic Avenida Paulista.

In an emotional speech, Mr. Lula thanked women and older voters for their support and praised the mobilisation of young people on the streets and on social media. “People went out to vote because we managed to convince them that their votes were extremely important to safeguarding democracy in the country,” he said. He also said he had learned many lessons from the election and promised to change his approach to governing, ensure greater public participation in government decisions and give digital communication a more prominent role during his fourth term. “The future begins today, and its name is youth. I salute the women who made all the difference. I salute the older people who made sacrifices and made their way to the polling stations to vote,” he said.

Mr. Lula secured an unprecedented comeback in the election. He trailed in the first round, receiving 45.16% of valid votes against 47.03% for Mr. Flávio. As the prospect of a Bolsonaro presidency caused a major concern among the young, especially about public education, healthcare and transport, millions of people joined weekly rallies across the country, pledging support for Mr. Lula and demanding protection of public services. On Sunday (October 25, 2026), Mr. Lula told his young supporters that their voices have been heard. “We will make increasing investment in in the Unified Health System, develop a national artificial intelligence system, continue to expand public universities and support the digital and creative economies,” Mr. Lula told his supporters with massive rounds of applause.

The turnaround after the first round of election on October 4 was not only historic but also dramatic. Mr. Lula’s official campaign team almost took a back seat as millions of people came out on streets and joined the social media campaign. The online mobilisation was led by federal deputy André Janones, who is not a member of the Workers Party but created a WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s Army”, where he issued “missions” to more than 10 million subscribers every day. The campaign focused its efforts on persuading undecided voters and those who had abstained in the first round. Mr. Lula’s young supporters, many of them teenagers, went on door-to-door campaigns to win over voters who had backed other candidates in the first round. On Sunday (October 25, 2026), abstention rates fell to their lowest levels since 2002.

With most opinion polls predicting a neck-to-neck race and some even giving an edge to Mr. Flavio till a few days back, the Workers’ Party shifted its messaging from a comparison of the candidates’ personal records to a forward-looking agenda centred on concrete promises. Following the first-round results, Mr. Lula changed his campaign team’s leadership and began announcing measures such as an increase in direct cash transfer benefits, a new debt-relief programme, a package of benefits for small entrepreneurs and a pledge to make public transport free on weekends.

Even as Mr. Lula made these promises to the electorate, his campaign faced a big challenge: Big Tech firms – from Meta to X and Google – openly supported Mr. Flavio’s campaign while suppressing advertising by Mr. Lula’s team. In his speech on Sunday (October 25, 2026), Mr. Lula said he had to overcome “interference” by digital platforms and pledged to regulate big tech companies in Brazil. “This election was one in which we had to overcome interference coming from outside and through digital platforms. We will have to regulate them,” Mr. Lula said. On October 16 after an expose in the Brazilian media, Meta had admitted that its artificial intelligence tool had blocked the generation of campaign material supporting Mr. Lula while allowing the same technology to be used by the Flávio campaign.

With this historic mobilisation of people and a record victory, Mr. Lula also seems to have defeated Mr. Trump, who has repeatedly made clear that his preferred candidate in the race was Mr. Flávio. Now, Mr. Lula’s victory has applied brakes on the growing wave of right-wing leaders in the region. But Mr. Trump is not in a mood to throw in the towel. On Sunday (October 25, 2026) night, Mr. Trump questioned Mr. Lula’s victory, comparing it to the 2020 U.S. election which he lost to Joe Biden and alleged that Brazil had followed the “Joe Biden playbook.”

“Bolsonaro had a big lead in the first round and was the clear favourite to win the second. But the communists never give up power once they get it,” Mr. Trump said, echoing the far-right’s strategy of questioning election results which do not go in their favour.

Mr. Flávio was singing the same tune on Sunday (October 25, 2026) night as he refused to accept the election result, announcing that he would seek the annulment of the election. He accused the Federal Supreme Federal of “changing the rules midway” after a judge ordered voting across the country to be extended until 7 p.m. when Mr. Lula complained about many right-wing mayors curtailing the bus services in the poor areas many cities. “It is impossible to recognise the election result in the context in which these things happened,” Mr. Flavio said, adding that his legal team would challenge the outcome.

It is a complete misreading of the mood in Brazil. After Mr. Lula finished his speech on Sunday (October 25, 2026) night, the crowd broke into a rendition of Brazil’s national independence song, sending a message to the far-right, Mr. Trump and Meta.

articles.title: Marine Le Pen, France’s far-right candidate, launches presidential bid
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: Marine Le Pen, France's far-right candidate to succeed President Emmanuel Macron, kicked off her campaign on Sunday (October 25, 2026) vowing to "restore the rule of law" if elected next year.

Ms. Le Pen, the frontrunner in the polls, seems to be benefiting from the convulsions France has been going through for weeks, which has seen violence flare on the side-lines of mass cost-of-living rallies.
"We are going to restore the rule of law," she said, after looting and arson erupted on the sidelines of demonstrations last weekend.

She was addressing 8,500 supporters of her nationalist, anti-immigration party in the city of Orleans, where Joan of Arc, revered by the far right as a symbol of national resistance, lifted an English siege in 1429.
"We are proposing for the country not a return to the past, but the dawn of a new era," the 58-year-old told the crowd, which broke into chants of "We're going to win, we're going to win."
Ms. Le Pen vowed to preserve France's cultural identity, from its language and traditions to its values and way of life, drawing thunderous cheers from supporters waving French flags.
Supporter Charlene Malingre, wearing a scarf emblazoned with the words "Marine President", said she was increasingly concerned about insecurity in France.
"I think Marine Le Pen could save France from the state it's in today, particularly when it comes to the economy, security and maintaining law and order," the 23-year-old told AFP.

More than 4,00,000 people marched in major French cities on Saturday (October 24, 2026) to protest against the rising cost of living. Clashes erupted after groups of masked protesters broke away from the demonstrations.
Police made more than 1,300 arrests and Interior Minister Laurent Nunez blamed much of the violence on "ultra-left" extremists.
Similar nationwide protests a week earlier also descended into unrest, following four weeks of student demonstrations over the poor state of France's schools.
Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu will hold talks with high school student organisations on Monday (October 26, 2026), a leader of one of the groups told AFP.

articles.title: Iran says officials from Saudi, Turkiye, Pakistan to visit Tehran for security talks
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-II & Current Affairs: Bilateral Agreements, Foreign Visits & UN/G20/BRICS
fullParagraphs: An Iranian official said on Monday (October 26, 2026) that senior officials from Saudi Arabia, Turkiye, and Pakistan will visit Tehran for talks over regional security, without specifying when the meeting would take place.

"As agreed, Saudi Defence Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani Army chief General Asim Munir and Turkish Intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin will participate in this meeting," said Ali Bagheri Kani, Deputy Secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council (SNSC).
He said the meeting will be held with Iran's Security chief Mohsen Rezaei.

"This four-party meeting in Tehran could represent an important and effective step towards building lasting regional security, and we hope this initiative will contribute to establishing a stable region," said Mr. Kani in an interview with state television, without elaborating.
He did not specify when the meeting would take place but said it was proposed during a visit by Pakistani Army chief Asim Munir to Tehran last week .

War has engulfed West Asia since February when the United States and Israel launched a wave of surprise attacks on Iran, while Washington and Tehran were in the midst of negotiations on Iran's nuclear programme.

An April ceasefire brought an end to the initial phase of intense bombardment but the two sides have continued to vie for control over the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to travel.

Iran has since claimed control over the strait and has regularly targeted vessels that attempt to cross without its authorisation, while the United States has imposed a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports.
Diplomatic efforts with the U.S. remain stalled, especially since the collapse of a June deal which laid out a pathway to a permanent settlement of the conflict.
The war has since spread across the region to include fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen.

articles.title: Can the new fortified potato variety the Centre is promoting help with India’s hidden hunger problem?
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Scientists at the ICAR-Central Potato Research Institute (CPRI) have developed a new potato variety called ‘kufri jamunia’ that has higher levels of anthocyanins, vitamin C, and certain micronutrients than regular potatoes. The Central government has been promoting it of late as a means to address hidden hunger, i.e. when people consume enough calories but still do not receive the necessary nutrients.

Usually, experts who fortify foods, focus on items like rice and iodised salt, which a large number of people in India consume, often throughout the year, thus ensuring the added nutrients are delivered to a significant chunk of the population. Kufri jamunia is however a potato, which people in India generally consume much less consistently than rice or salt, and the micronutrient intake depends on preparation methods and how the body absorbs them.

Kufri jamunia offers nutritional advantages, but they are substantial in some aspects more than others. Questions also linger about its ability to resist disease and retain nutrients through different Indian cooking methods.

The variety reportedly has a mealy texture. In one CPRI assessment involving 64 people, 95% rated its overall acceptability ‘good to excellent’ and 56% said its taste was very good. This study cohort, though, is too small to generalise the results. CPRI researchers themselves have proposed that kufri jamunia can be used in curries, parathas, soups, baked goods, and dehydrated flours.

Importantly, kufri jamunia potatoes also have purple skin and flesh, which could affect consumer interest. Research on other biofortified foods has already shown that while people are generally willing to pay modest premiums — the national average cost of ordinary potatoes purchased wholesale is around ₹17/kg — whether they accept a new variety depends on its appearance, their awareness, taste, and of course local preferences.

The CPRI team developed the kufri jamunia variety by crossing two potato lines, MS/8-1148 and CP4242, in 2015. MS/8-1148 is high in vitamin C whereas CP4242 had purple skin and flesh. The result, formally called MSP/16-307, could naturally accumulate higher concentrations of specific nutrients as it grew. The team then conducted trials, including multi-location testing, in 2021-2023.

Based on the trial data, the Central Sub-Committee on Crop Standards, Notification and Release of Varieties for Horticultural Crops approved the variety in mid-2024 and the government notified it in November that year. The variety’s plants produce 10-12 medium to large tubers each and mature in around 90 days. The purple colour comes from anthocyanins — organic compounds also found in jamun and blueberries.

According to the Press Information Bureau, 100 g of kufri jamunia flesh contains around 42.75 mg of vitamin C (versus 23.15 mg in regular potatoes), 42.05 mg of anthocyanins, 2.28 mg of zinc (versus 0.28 mg), 3.22 mg of iron (versus 0.57 mg), and 161 micrograms of carotenoids. And per the CPRI team’s findings themselves, published in Potato Journal in 2025, 100 g of kufri jamunia was found to have a range of carotenoid levels, from 15.6 micrograms in Kanpur to 298.4 micrograms in Raipur, during the multi-location trials. Kufri jamunia also contains slightly less zinc than kufri neelkanth and slightly less iron than kufri manik; the latter are other coloured potato varieties developed at the Institute.

Anthocyanins are known to have antioxidant properties, although whether the same benefits will accrue when delivered by kufri jamunia potatoes is not known. And in the absence of similar studies, the same caveat goes for iron and zinc.

A 2016 study in Food Chemistry examined purple-fleshed potatoes and reported that steaming and microwaving generally preserved more of the nutritional substances than stir-frying did. However, again, research specific to kufri jamunia is not available.
Nutrient availability and delivery constitutes one half of a biofortification programme; the other half is determined by cultivation.

At the Modipuram research station, according to the Potato Journal paper, the team recorded an average yield of 49.01 tonnes per hectare after three months, across three seasons, whereas subsequent multi-location trials, including at Modipuram, recorded an overall mean of 31.96 tonnes per hectare across north (36.77 tonnes), central (33.79 tonnes), and eastern (25.91 tonnes) India.

articles.title: AI’s costs fall unevenly across workers; IIT Madras paper flags surveillance, work stress
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: The costs of artificial intelligence (AI) adoption fall unevenly across workers, with entry-level jobs particularly at risk, according to a whitepaper by the Centre for Responsible AI (CeRAI) at the Indian Institute of Technology Madras (IIT-Madras).

“The entry-level career pipeline is especially at risk,” the paper says, highlighting differences in how AI affects entry-level and experienced workers, formal and informal workers, urban and rural workers, and employees in micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and large firms.

Titled ‘How AI Is Reconfiguring Work in India: A Task-Based Framework for Understanding Augmentation, Displacement, New Roles and the Changing Structure of Jobs’, the paper examines how AI automates tasks within jobs and how this can lead to changes in work, new roles or displacement.

The paper identifies differences in firms’ ability to adopt AI. Large companies can absorb the fixed costs of integrating and customising advanced models, while MSMEs depend more on narrow, subsidised tools. It also flags differences between English and regional-language work, noting that Indian-language AI performs less well on nuanced, code-switched conversations.

Automation is also creating new roles, including robot operators and AI escalation specialists. However, the paper says its evidence does not systematically track whether such roles offer stable employment or piecework, a distinction that affects how much of the productivity gains reaches workers.

The paper says its framework is “largely silent” on changes in job quality because Indian evidence is limited. It identifies wages, workplace monitoring, work intensity, stress and burnout, career progression, the quality of human interaction and responsibility for errors as areas requiring further study.

Among the questions it raises is whether AI will bring new forms of performance tracking, such as scoring the calls handled by BPO employees after AI has taken over routine queries, or using dashboards to track productivity among MSME shop-floor workers.

It also asks whether AI could leave workers handling a more demanding stream of exceptions after automating less-intensive tasks. The authors caution that the available Indian sources do not systematically measure these dimensions.

Junior roles have traditionally served as apprenticeships, with routine tasks helping workers develop the judgement needed for senior positions, the paper says. If AI automates tasks such as password resets, basic contract reviews and boilerplate coding, it raises questions about how new employees will acquire that experience.
The issue is particularly relevant to India’s IT, business process outsourcing (BPO), finance and professional-services sectors, which have historically hired large numbers of entry-level graduates.

One possible response is to redesign junior roles around supervising and correcting AI rather than performing routine tasks. But the paper says it remains an open question whether firms will redesign career paths or simply hire fewer junior employees.

The paper notes that its framework relies largely on formal-sector evidence, despite informal work accounting for a substantially larger share of India’s workforce than the formal jobs examined in detail.

articles.title: Amid row, Keralam’s UDF govt says cost of generic SMA drug can be cut further
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: The Congress-led United Democratic Front (UDF) government in Keralam on Monday strongly defended the switch to a generic drug for patients with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) and said it would try to further reduce the price of the drug.

Speaking in the State Legislative Assembly, Health Minister K. Muraleedharan announced that the UDF government’s aim, eventually, was to offer medicines free of cost to all SMA patients. The matter will be discussed with Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan and an announcement will be made in due course, Mr. Muraleedharan said.

The Health Minister was responding to an adjournment motion moved by the CPI(M)-led Opposition Left Democratic Front (LDF) with regard to the controversy over the generic SMA drug and the unconnected development where the government had formed a 16-member task force with the aim of establishing a ‘Kerala Holistic Model for Health, Wellness and Longevity.’

While the Opposition accused the government of launching ‘clinical trials’ on SMA patients and pushing a corporatisation agenda in the health sector through the task force, Chief Minister Mr. Satheesan said both decisions were taken in the best interests of the people.
The Assembly witnessed a sharp confrontation between the ruling and Opposition fronts over the two issues, leading to a walkout by the latter after the adjournment motion was rejected.
With regard to the generic SMA drug, Mr. Satheesan said the government decision gave patients access to a generic drug that cost just ₹15,000 when the branded version cost ₹6.5 lakh for 12 days.

The generic alternative, marketed by Natco Pharma, had the support of court orders and statutory clearances from government agencies concerned, he said. “It has brought immense relief to the families of the patients. Our belief is that the price can be reduced further, to ₹9,000,” Mr. Satheesan said. He also congratulated Mr. Muraleedharan and the Health Department for taking the decision.

However, Leader of the Opposition Pinarayi Vijayan said the government was “misleading everyone” by depicting the LDF as being opposed to generic drugs and that it favoured the costly Risdiplam, marketed by Roche Pharmaceuticals. Mr. Vijayan said the LDF has always encouraged generic medicines. “But here, the issue pertained to clinical trials of the SMA drug,” he said.
The LDF also targeted the composition of the task force; specifically the inclusion of Deepak Singhal, a former Uttar Pradesh Chief Secretary.

Mr. Vijayan said that Mr. Singhal’s links to Global Trade and Technology Council (India) (GTTCI Healthcare Ventures) was “a matter of concern.” Corporates viewed the health sector as a milch cow and his presence on the task force illustrated the UDF’s “corporatisation agenda” for the sector, he said.

The Chief Minister, however, swept aside the charge, stating that the 16-member task force was composed of "knowledge partners.” Its aim was to devise strategies to reduce healthcare costs and ensure early detection of diseases and their prevention. This was important at a time when investment giants such as Blackstone have entered the State’s health sector and medical bills in private hospitals were soaring, making such institutions inaccessible to the general public, he said.

Earlier, K. Premkumar of the CPI(M), K. Rajan of the CPI, and P.K. Praveen of the RJD had moved the adjournment motion. They sought a discussion in the House on the perils faced by the State’s health sector arising from the government decisions to include representatives of “private hospitals, laboratories and pharma companies” in the task force and the concerns over clinical trials related to the SMA drug.

articles.title: Seven caveats in the claim about turning mercury into gold with nuclear fusion
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: A San Francisco-based company named Marathon Fusion announced on October 21 that it had ‘converted’ mercury into gold in an experiment in September and that it had achieved a production rate tenfold greater than a record reported by CERN in 2025.

The company has also proposed a programme in which mercury-198 is exposed to high-energy neutrons produced by nuclear fusion — in an existing power plant — converting it into radioactive mercury-197, which subsequently decays into stable gold-197. In a preprint paper uploaded to the arXiv repository in July 2025, Marathon scientists had predicted this process could produce roughly 2 tonnes of gold annually for every gigawatt (GW) of thermal fusion power.

articles.title: The other face of air pollution | Excerpt from The Nitrogen Bomb by Jacob Koshy
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: The Indo-Gangetic Plain (IGP) stretches across northern India in a 2,500-kilometre arc from Pakistan to Bangladesh and is home to nearly half a billion people. It is one of the most intensively farmed landscapes on earth, and by every atmospheric measure, one of the most chemically burdened places that has been peopled for millennia. What Odén [Svante Odén, the Swedish scientist who first linked acid rain and its wide-ranging environmental harms] mapped in Scandinavia — nitrogen from farms, nitrogen oxides from engines, ammonia reacting with acids to produce particles that choke lungs and kill quietly — is happening here, now, on a scale and at a speed that would make Europe’s post-war industrial peak antediluvian.

In 2025, I reported on a study by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a think tank, that said secondary pollutants, particularly ammonium sulphate that forms when sulphur dioxide from coal plants meets ammonia from fertilised fields, were responsible for nearly one-third of India’s PM2.5 pollution burden.

I remember writing then, trying to explain to readers who, like me, had been led to believe that Delhi’s winters were a problem of primary pollutants from stubble fires and diesel exhaust: ‘Primary pollutants are those that result from the burning of fossil fuels from automobiles, coal plants and organic matter.’ The distinction matters because it changes everything about how you think about solutions. During Delhi’s most polluted winter months, the CREA analysis found, it was secondary pollutants that constituted nearly 41 per cent of all fine particles in the winter air. The problem isn’t what you can see coming out of a tailpipe or a chimney but what is being silently assembled in the atmosphere, molecule by molecule and reaction by reaction.

The one-third figure, however, carries a chemist’s caveat. Professor Srinidhi Balasubramanian, who teaches in the Department of Environmental Science and Engineering at the Indian Institute of Technology Bombay, has spent close to two decades studying ammonia as an agricultural air pollutant — first in the maize belt of the American Midwest, at the University of Illinois, following it up at the University of Minnesota, and now across the Indo-Gangetic Plain.

She begins her air-quality exposition to me with a line borrowed from a Class VII science textbook. ‘Acid plus base forms a salt,’ she told me. ‘It is as simple as that.’ The acids are the familiar villains — nitrogen oxides from combustion and the sulphur dioxide from coal that is yellowing the Taj Mahal. The base, ‘the single most dominant one, by any stretch’, is ammonia, and the source of that ammonia is overwhelmingly agricultural. Her 2021 work put the farming share at roughly 80 per cent globally, and India, she reckons, at 80 to 85 per cent, the rest leaking from fertiliser plants and industry.

If you look at it, it is the other side of the coin that Odén puzzled over in Scandinavia. The problem he had identified was acids and what she is drawing attention to is the base. ‘This is the other face of acid rain,’ Balasubramanian said. ‘As acid rain reduces, your PM problem exaggerates.’ Where Smith’s Manchester and Odén’s Sweden carried a surplus of acid and watched it fall, the fertilised plains of northern India carry, on top of their acids, an overwhelming surplus of the base — and the salt the two make is settling into human lungs. Her own modelling refines the arithmetic behind the CREA figure: ammonia acting alone accounts for about a quarter of India’s PM2.5, she estimates; bundled with the nitrogen oxides and coal-derived sulphur it reacts with, the inorganic secondary fraction climbs to roughly 40 per cent, and with the organic secondaries added, the national balance tips to something like 45 per cent primary against 55 per cent secondary.

Dr. Balasubramanian is among the small group of Indian scientists who have been tracing the chemistry of what happens over the IGP, across multiple institutions. The foundational work began at the Indian Institute of Technology, Kanpur (IIT-K) with Sachchida Nand Tripathi, who in 2003 established what would become the National Aerosol Facility, the first of its kind in India.

Kanpur is almost the geographic centre of the IGP and from here his group built the long-term datasets on trace gases and aerosol properties that first revealed the seasonal patterns of IGP pollution. A 2014 study from his lab documented four years of continuous measurements of SO2, nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, and ozone at Kanpur, establishing the winter loading patterns that make IGP winters chemically unlike any other season anywhere. Cold temperatures push the chemical equilibrium towards the particle phase, and the planetary boundary layer — the lid of air above the city — often compresses below 400 metres, trapping precursor gases until they react. Nitrogen oxides from vehicles and industry peak in winter, the group found, at exactly the moment when the atmospheric conditions for converting them to ammonium nitrate particles are most favourable.

articles.title: Why did Tinder’s scam detection fail, and what should Indian users do?
articles.examRelevance: GS Paper-III & Prelims: ISRO/NASA Missions, Defense Updates, Tech & Climate Reports
fullParagraphs: Earlier in October, U.S. lawmakers revealed how users of dating apps were being exposed to serious financial and physical risks. They pinned this to the outdated AI stack in these applications.

In an investigation centred around the Match Group, the lawmakers found that the algorithm matched U.S. users of dating apps like Tinder and Hinge with scammers. The report, titled ‘Outmatched: Tinder, Scammers, and Match Group’s Efforts to Catch Up’, highlighted that users connected with nearly 1.5 million scammers on these two popular dating applications in the first nine months of 2025.
At the core of these disturbing findings were outdated machine learning models installed to detect bad actors. These hadn’t been updated in years, per the report.

This information came from internal documents that the Match Group shared with the committee, led by senator Maggie Hassan. As the accuracy of scam detection dropped, Tinder began depending on other measures that it knew were often ineffective.
“In fact, Match Group knew that Tinder was more likely to show a profile if it belonged to a scammer or other bad actor rather than a regular user,” stated an official press release about the report.
However, the investigation acknowledged that the Match Group later put in place new safety measures, such as an AI model in Tinder this year that was designed to detect scammers and bad actors.

The report included statements from victims who described how romance scammers cheated them out of tens of thousands of dollars after building a relationship with them on the dating apps. A common trend was to cite a major emergency in order to pressure the victim into sending over money. Using the victims’ phone number and/or email ID, the scammers would proceed to harass them online until the victim sometimes paid them in the hopes of de-escalating their aggression.
Another type of scam involved the same malicious user operating as different people on the same dating app, to ensnare more victims.

The report pointed to an inconsistent dating app AI strategy, where patchy machine learning systems led to heavy caseloads and “overwhelmed” human moderators who were unable to focus on visibly risky accounts. Per a document from the Match Group itself, Tinder could have better tackled dangerous accounts by building better AI signals or reducing its reliance on manual rules.

“In practice, these moderation lapses meant that bad actors that reached moderation were not immediately banned and instead may have continued to interact with and harm legitimate users until the platform gathered additional evidence,” explained the report.

A bouquet of dating apps come under the Match Group, including Tinder, Hinge, Match (formerly Match.com), Plenty of Fish, and more such offerings catering to users in diverse countries and cultural communities.

In other words, a security lapse in one app comes with serious implications for the users of other Match Group-owned apps. Tinder and Hinge are popular in India as well, claiming the top ranks in terms of downloads via app marketplaces.

articles.title: Old values, new avenues: On India-Poland ties
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: Sixteen years after his visit as Poland’s Prime Minister, Donald Tusk’s travel to Delhi and Bengaluru last week was to signal a renewed desire to work closely with India. Mr. Tusk’s visit, two months ahead of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s trip to Brussels to sign the India-European Union (EU) Free Trade Agreement , indicated one part of his agenda. Both sides agreed that it was time to develop trade, currently worth just $6 billion, to double its size by 2030. Mr. Tusk’s last visit to India was in 2017, as President of the European Council for the EU-India summit, and it is fitting that his trip was just as the FTA is finalised and ratified after years of delays. Another area of increased India-Poland collaboration is in technology, AI and defence hardware, critical minerals, renewable and nuclear energy given Poland’s expertise in the last few decades and India’s capacity for scale. As the EU’s sixth largest economy, Poland has officially crossed the $1 trillion GDP (nominal terms) milestone. Its $120-billion-dollar tech economy is also gaining global interest. A large part of Polish machinery and parts is exported to Germany, which in turn has a growing share of Indian imports, and India could consider more trilateral collaborations for manufacturing and mining technology. The two sides agreed to establish a “Defence Industry Dialogue” and explore a dialogue on counter-terrorism cooperation. Finally, the Modi-Tusk talks focused on geopolitics, particularly the ongoing war in Ukraine. The war’s impact, especially on the Global South, has been a concern for India, and the Modi government’s initiative to work on an agreement acceptable to Kyiv and Moscow on grain exports and seafarers’ safety was discussed. The four-pronged plan, announced by External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar during his September visit to Warsaw, won Mr. Tusk’s support.

At the India-Poland Business Forum in Bengaluru, Mr. Tusk, who was accompanied by a Polish business delegation, said the challenge now was in “translating” the talks and MoUs signed into actual joint ventures between businesses. Apart from the distance and geographies, there is the matter of trust, given India’s defence engagement with Russia and Poland’s defence ties with Pakistan. Poland is credited with training Pakistan’s Air Force in its early years; a mutual defence cooperation agreement was signed in 2018. India has a unique and enduring partnership with Russia, and New Delhi is unlikely to accept Warsaw’s strictures over its military engagement and exercises with Russia that caused a controversy earlier this year during the Polish Foreign Minister’s visit. It is essential for Delhi and Warsaw to complete the confidentiality of classified information that is still being negotiated and draw up the parameters of future cooperation based on realities. Mr. Tusk’s statement that India and Poland today have no “conflicts of interest” is a significant aspiration, for two countries that share old values, and new avenues of partnership.

articles.title: Wicked surprise: On the northeast monsoon
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: As India recovers from a monsoon-deficit year , there is both hope and trepidation regarding the prospects for that ‘other monsoon’, or the ‘northeast monsoon’ . While contributing only around a quarter of India’s annual rainfall, it is largely focused on the south-east peninsula regions of Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, coastal Andhra Pradesh, Rayalaseema, south interior Karnataka and Keralam. The southwest monsoon, influenced by a strengthening El Niño , has already left its desiccating mark. Rainfall from June-September was 759.4 mm against 868.6 mm, a 12.6% deficit, the driest in 11 years. This has impacted kharif sowing and is reflected in food inflation.

The India Meteorological Department (IMD) has said that this year, the northeast monsoon rainfall, spanning October to December, would likely be ‘normal’ , meaning in line with a 50-year average and within a 12% error window. Most parts of the country, it said, are expected to receive below-normal rainfall, except some areas of northwest India and southern parts of peninsular India, where rainfall is likely to be normal to above-normal. The wide error window, however, is far less precise than its forecasts for the southwest monsoon with its margin of 5%, and can sometimes make the northeast monsoon the bearer of nasty surprises. For instance, December 1, 2015, saw the city of Chennai deluged by its heaviest rainfall in 24-hours in over a century ; at least 500 lives were lost and 18 lakh people displaced in the State. That year and the present are linked by a common thread: a powerful El Niño. Associated with the heating up of the Central Pacific, the El Niño is linked to the drying up of the southwest monsoon rains but also yoked — not always — with a vigorous northeast monsoon. Other than in 2015, several El Niño years, such as 1997 and 2009, have been associated with above-normal rainfall between October and December in Tamil Nadu though El Niño years, such as 2002 and 1982, saw a poor northeast monsoon (and a predictably bad southwest monsoon). While the climate mechanisms linking a vigorous northeast monsoon and El Niño are still to be fully understood, it appears the warming patterns of the El Niño tend to deflect rain-bearing cyclonic circulations in unpredictable ways. Therefore, the Centre and the southern States ought to take enough precautions: from clearing up stormwater drains, fortifying shelters, making provisions for infrastructure damage and tightening weather warning forecasts to prepare for torrents.

articles.title: In the crossfire: on India and the Saudi-Houthi conflict
articles.examRelevance: UPSC & State PSC Mains / Essay: Deep Analytical Core Summary & Vocabulary
fullParagraphs: The killing of an Indian national in a Houthi attack on Saudi Arabia’s Dammam airport is a grim reminder of the dangers the kingdom’s Indian community faces as the conflict between Riyadh and Yemen’s Shia militants escalates. Since the fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis resumed in July, at least two Indians have been killed and 14 others wounded. On Thursday, the Houthis claimed that a yacht with 14 Indians was targeted by Saudi forces near Yemen’s Zuqar island in the Red Sea and that rescue operations were under way. As the Houthis, who control parts of Northern Yemen and its entire Red Sea coast, step up attacks on Saudi infrastructure, including oil facilities and airports, Indians, who are the kingdom’s largest expat community, risk getting caught in the crossfire. With flights disrupted, thousands of Indian pilgrims are stranded. India has condemned Houthi attacks, saying that it “stands in solidarity” with Saudi Arabia. With no end in sight to the fighting and a high possibility of Israel and the U.S. resuming their Iran strikes, further violence and instability in West Asia could make India’s choices increasingly difficult.

The Saudi-Houthi conflict dates back to the Houthi takeover of Sana’a, Yemen’s capital, in 2014. A year later, Saudi Arabia began bombing Yemen to drive the Houthis out. But years of Saudi bombing of one of the poorest Arab countries have proved counterproductive; the Houthis consolidated support among the tribes of northern Yemen and built a powerful territorial army and naval force. The Saudi-Houthi ceasefire of 2022 collapsed in July 2026 after Saudi Arabia recklessly bombed Sana’a airport, to prevent an Iranian plane with a Houthi delegation from landing. The Houthis subsequently began attacking Saudi Arabia’s critical infrastructure, and launched a ground offensive against the Saudi-backed forces in Yemen. The Houthi attacks pose the biggest security challenge to Mohammed bin Salman, Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince and the main architect of the war on Yemen, in decades. Massive Saudi air strikes have neither defeated the Houthis nor restored the kingdom’s deterrence. With its wealth, natural resources, infrastructure and tenuous palace politics, the kingdom remains exposed to Houthi missile and drone attacks, with few good options for a way out. India must prepare a contingency plan for worst-case scenarios. Its immediate priority should be to evacuate stranded Indian pilgrims. It should also articulate a stronger position for stability and work with Arab countries and Tehran to push for a diplomatic settlement to the Iran crisis . For peace to prevail in the Persian Gulf, the guns directed at Iran must first fall silent.
